lessons.title: Reading the Text
lessons.notes_html:
Pre-reading

Before Islam, Arabia was a land of great natural beauty but of social and moral disorder. In the fifth and sixth centuries, mankind stood on the verge of chaos: the civilization built over four thousand years had started crumbling, and people lived in ignorance, superstition, cruelty and injustice, worshipping idols instead of one God. The Arabs themselves were gifted — they possessed remarkable memory and eloquence, expressed in poetry — but they lacked divine guidance, which is why the text presents the coming of the Rasoolullah as the lifting of humanity from ignorance into the light of faith.

Pre-reading

Islam changed people's lives completely: it replaced idol-worship and superstition with the Oneness of Allah (Tauheed) and the unity of mankind, destroyed the nexus of ignorance and disbelief, and set up a noble conception of life. The text says this produced a thorough transformation of man and society, raising man to the highest possible level in both spiritual and worldly domains, and giving humanity a perfect model to follow in the life and character of the Rasoolullah.

Pre-reading

Hazrat Muhammad (peace be upon him) is the last Rasool of Allah. He was born in Makkah Mukarramah, received the first revelation in the cave of Hira, and proclaimed Tauheed and the unity of mankind for twenty-three years. The text quotes the Quran (33:45-46): he was sent as a witness, a bearer of good news and a warner, and as one inviting to Allah by His permission, and as a light-giving torch.

Pre-reading

The world's major religions include Islam (Hazrat Muhammad, peace be upon him, as the last Rasool), Christianity (Hazrat Isa/Jesus), Judaism (Hazrat Musa/Moses), Hinduism (with figures such as Rama and Krishna in its tradition), Buddhism (Gautama Buddha) and Sikhism (Guru Nanak). The unit itself focuses on Islam, and its message of Tauheed, compassion and the unity of mankind, which the text presents as guidance for all humanity.

While-reading

A fair for poetical competitions was held at Ukaz every year. The text says the Arabs were an eloquent people whose eloquence and memory found expression in poetry, and it quotes Hammad telling Caliph Walid bin Yazid that he could recite, for each letter of the alphabet, one hundred long poems composed exclusively by poets before the promulgation of Islam.

While-reading

When he was thirty-eight years of age, he spent most of his time in solitude and meditation in the cave of Hira, retiring there with food and water and spending days and weeks in remembrance of Allah. The period of waiting then came to a close when he was bestowed with Nabuwat and Hazrat Jibril (Gabriel) brought the first revelation.

While-reading

They sent a delegation to the Rasoolullah's kind and caring uncle, Hazrat Abu Talib. They told him either to restrain the Rasoolullah from preaching Allah's message or to face their enmity. Finding himself in a dilemma, Abu Talib sent for his nephew and explained the situation, and received the memorable reply about the sun in the right hand and the moon in the left.

While-reading

In 'The 100: A Ranking of the Most Influential Persons in History', Michael H. Hart wrote that Muhammad (peace be upon him) was responsible for both the theology of Islam and its main ethical and moral principles, played the key role in proselytizing the new faith and establishing its religious practices, and, as the driving force behind the Arab conquests, may well rank as the most influential political leader of all times, with the seventh-century Arab conquests continuing to play an important role in human history down to the present day.

Reading and Critical Thinking A

The description presents Makkah Mukarramah as a place of unparalleled charm and beauty — trackless deserts of sand dunes under the dazzling rays of the tropical sun, and a starry sky that excited the imagination of poets and travellers — about fifty miles from the Red Sea. This setting makes the reader feel that something momentous belongs in such a striking land: a remote, poetic, desert city, far from the great empires, yet chosen as the birthplace of the Rasoolullah. The geography thus underlines the historical importance: a universal message arose not from a capital of power but from a small desert town, which makes its worldwide influence seem all the more remarkable.

Reading and Critical Thinking A

It suggests that pre-Islamic Arab culture was rich in oral and poetic tradition even though it lacked divine guidance. The Arabs possessed a remarkable memory and were an eloquent people; their eloquence and memory found expression in poetry, with yearly poetical competitions at Ukaz, and a single reciter claiming one hundred long poems for each letter of the alphabet from pre-Islamic poets alone. The emphasis shows a people of great linguistic and cultural talent — which is why the text notes it is no wonder Allah chose the Arabic language for His final dispensation and the preservation of His Word — while also implying that this talent existed alongside the ignorance the new message would remove.

Reading and Critical Thinking A

The anecdote provides concrete evidence for the Arabs' extraordinary memory and poetic culture: Hammad told Caliph Walid bin Yazid that he could recite, for each letter of the alphabet, one hundred long poems, without counting short pieces, all composed by pre-Islamic poets. Its importance is that it turns a general claim ('remarkable memory') into a vivid, memorable proof, and it justifies the next point in the text — that Allah chose Arabic for His final message — because a language with such a powerful poetic tradition was a fitting vessel for the Quran.

Reading and Critical Thinking A

The text describes a civilization that had taken four thousand years to grow but had started crumbling, with mankind on the verge of chaos in the fifth and sixth centuries, until a new message lifted humanity from ignorance into the light of faith. A parallel is the decline of the Roman Empire, where political decay and moral disorder were followed by renewal through a new faith and new institutions; another is the European Dark Ages followed by the Renaissance, when learning and art revived a declining civilization. The common pattern is that decline creates the conditions for renewal: when old systems crumble, a powerful new idea — a faith, a philosophy, a reform movement — can transform society thoroughly, just as the text says Islam transformed man and society.

Reading and Critical Thinking A

He faced determined opposition from the pagan Arabs, because his belief threatened their dominance in society. They mounted pressure on him and his followers, wanting them to renounce their cause and return to idol-worshipping, and they sent a delegation to his uncle Hazrat Abu Talib demanding that he restrain his nephew or face their enmity. His answer — that even if they put the sun in his right hand and the moon in his left, he would not abandon the proclamation of Tauheed, and would establish the true faith or perish in the attempt — shows the scale of the challenge: he risked his safety, his family ties and his life for the message.

Reading and Critical Thinking A

Spiritually, he proclaimed the Oneness of Allah (Tauheed) and the unity of mankind, destroyed the nexus of superstition, ignorance and disbelief, and set up a noble conception of life, leading mankind to the light of faith and divine bliss; his deep faith in Allah, his love for humanity and the nobility of his character made his life a perfect model to follow. In worldly terms, he was the driving force behind the Arab conquests, which created an everlasting impression on human history, and Michael H. Hart ranks him as possibly the most influential political leader of all times. The text sums this up as a thorough transformation of man and society, owed to his faith, his love for humanity and his character.

Reading and Critical Thinking A

The verse — 'O Nabi! Surely, We have sent you as a witness, and bearer of good news and warner. And as the one inviting to Allah by His permission, and as a light-giving torch' — sums up his whole mission in four roles. As a witness, he testifies to the truth; as a bearer of good news, he promises divine bliss to believers; as a warner, he warns against disbelief and wrongdoing; and as a light-giving torch, he guides humanity out of the darkness of ignorance into the light of faith. This matches the text's account exactly: he was raised to lift humanity from ignorance, to proclaim Tauheed, and to be a model whose morals and character, in Hazrat Ayesha's words, are an embodiment of the Holy Quran.

Reading and Critical Thinking A

Write down the examples and the evidences supporting your inferences. The author views the pre-Islamic Arabs with respect for their natural gifts but as people living in ignorance and in need of guidance. Evidence for their gifts: they 'possessed a remarkable memory and were an eloquent people'; their eloquence found expression in poetry; a fair for poetical competitions was held at Ukaz every year; and Hammad claimed one hundred long poems per letter of the alphabet from pre-Islamic poets alone. Evidence for their condition: in the fifth and sixth centuries mankind 'stood on the verge of chaos' and civilization was 'crumbling'; the pagan Arabs later opposed the new message, pressured the Rasoolullah and his followers, and demanded they renounce their cause and return to idol-worshipping. The author's inference is therefore balanced: a talented, poetic people, but one whose society needed the transformation Islam brought.

Reading and Critical Thinking B

The main idea of paragraph 5 is that the time of waiting was over: filled with profound compassion for humanity and a pressing urge to eradicate wrong beliefs, social evils, cruelty and injustice, the Rasoolullah (peace be upon him) was bestowed with Nabuwat when Hazrat Jibril brought him the first revelation in the cave of Hira — 'Read in the name of thy Lord Who created...' (Quran 96:1-5).

Reading and Critical Thinking B

The supporting details are: his heart was overflowing with profound compassion for humanity; he had a pressing urge to eradicate wrong beliefs, social evils, cruelty and injustice; the moment had arrived for him to be bestowed with Nabuwat; one day in the cave of Hira, Hazrat Jibril came and conveyed Allah's message; and the message itself is quoted — the first five verses of Surah Al-Alaq commanding reading in the name of the Lord Who created man and taught him what he knew not.

Reading and Critical Thinking C

Hazrat Muhammad (peace be upon him), the last Rasool of Allah, is presented as the Saviour of Mankind, whose life and teachings transformed humanity. Born in Makkah Mukarramah, a land of deserts, dunes and a starry sky, he grew up among Arabs famed for remarkable memory and eloquence, whose poetry flourished at the yearly fair of Ukaz. In the fifth and sixth centuries, when civilization was crumbling and mankind stood on the verge of chaos, he spent his thirty-eighth year in solitude and meditation in the cave of Hira, where he received the first revelation (Quran 96:1-5) and was bestowed with Nabuwat. For twenty-three years he proclaimed the Oneness of Allah (Tauheed) and the unity of mankind, destroying superstition, ignorance and disbelief despite fierce opposition from the pagan Arabs, who pressed his uncle Abu Talib to stop him; his reply — that he would not abandon Tauheed even if the sun were placed in his right hand and the moon in his left — showed his firm resolve. His faith, love for humanity and noble character elevated man to the highest level spiritually and worldly, and historians such as Michael H. Hart rank him among the most influential figures in history; as the Quran says (33:45-46), he was sent as a witness, a bearer of good news, a warner, and a light-giving torch.

lessons.title: Vocabulary
lessons.notes_html:
Vocabulary A

Use a dictionary to find the following information for each word: pronunciation, dictionary meaning, part of speech. Words: imagination, remarkable, composed, preservation. imagination — Pronunciation: /ih-maj-ih-NAY-shun/ (British: /ɪˌmædʒɪˈneɪʃn/). Dictionary meaning: the ability to form pictures or ideas in the mind of things not present or not real. Part of speech: noun. — remarkable — Pronunciation: /ri-MAHR-kuh-bul/ (/rɪˈmɑːkəbl/). Meaning: worthy of attention; extraordinary or unusual. Part of speech: adjective. — composed — Pronunciation: /kuhm-POHZD/ (/kəmˈpəʊzd/). Meaning: (of a person) calm and in control of feelings; also: formed or made up of parts. Part of speech: adjective (past participle of 'compose' used as an adjective). — preservation — Pronunciation: /prez-er-VAY-shun/ (/ˌprezəˈveɪʃn/). Meaning: the act of keeping something in its original state or in good condition, or protecting it from harm or loss. Part of speech: noun.

Vocabulary B

The dictionary definitions largely confirm the inferences drawn from the text. 'Imagination' in the text ('its starry sky has excited the imagination of poets') matches the dictionary sense of forming pictures and ideas in the mind — the poets pictured wonders under the stars. 'Remarkable' ('a remarkable memory') matches 'worthy of attention, extraordinary' — the Arabs' memory was indeed extraordinary, as the Hammad anecdote proves. 'Preservation' ('the preservation of His Word') matches 'keeping something in its original state and protecting it from harm' — the Quran was preserved exactly. Where an inference was only approximate (for example, guessing 'composed' means 'calm'), the dictionary refines it: 'composed' can mean calm and controlled, but also 'made up of parts', so the context must decide which sense applies.

Vocabulary C

1. Rewrite (prefix re- + write): I had to rewrite my essay after the teacher pointed out my mistakes. 2. Teacher (teach + suffix -er): Our teacher explained the lesson clearly. 3. Unhappy (prefix un- + happy): He felt unhappy when his team lost the match. 4. Kindness (kind + suffix -ness): Her kindness towards the poor impressed everyone. 5. Disagreement (prefix dis- + agree + suffix -ment): Their disagreement over the plan was settled by discussion.

Vocabulary D

Use a dictionary to find and write the different word patterns for the word 'advocate'. Complete the chart by identifying the correct forms of the word 'advocate' and its related forms. Base word: advocate. Noun form: advocate (a person who publicly supports a cause, e.g. an advocate of free education); advocacy (the act of supporting a cause). Verb form: advocate (to publicly support an idea or cause). Adjective form: there is no commonly used adjective form of 'advocate' in standard English (the rare form 'advocative' is not in general use and should not be forced into the chart). Adverb form: there is likewise no standard adverb form. Note: the chart cannot be filled for all four columns from standard usage — the honest completion is noun and verb forms only, with adjective and adverb marked as not applicable.

Vocabulary E

Noun (advocate): She is a strong advocate of girls' education. Noun (advocacy): His advocacy for clean drinking water improved the whole village. Verb (advocate): We advocate tolerance and respect for all religions. (No model sentences are given for adjective or adverb forms, because 'advocate' has no standard adjective or adverb form — see Vocabulary D.)

lessons.title: Grammar Focus
lessons.notes_html:
Grammar A

Identify and label nouns, verbs and conjunctions in the given sentences. (The task also covers the other parts of speech taught in the unit; all are labelled below.) i. 'The quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog.' Nouns: fox, dog. Verb: jumps. Adjectives: quick, brown, lazy. Preposition: over. Article: The, the. — ii. 'After the storm, the sky was clear and bright.' Nouns: storm, sky. Verb: was (linking verb). Adjectives: clear, bright. Conjunction: and. Preposition: After. — iii. 'She quickly finished her homework before dinner.' Pronoun: She, her. Adverb: quickly. Verb: finished. Nouns: homework, dinner. Preposition: before. — iv. 'Wow! That was an incredible match.' Interjection: Wow! Pronoun: That. Verb: was. Article: an. Adjective: incredible. Noun: match. — v. 'Because it was raining, they decided to stay indoors.' Conjunction: Because (subordinating). Pronoun: it, they. Verb: was, decided, stay. Adverb: indoors.

Grammar B

1. Wow! She quickly put her blue bag on the table, and she smiled. (Interjection: Wow! Pronoun: She, she. Adverb: quickly. Verb: put, smiled. Noun: bag, table. Adjective: blue. Preposition: on. Conjunction: and.) 2. Oh! He happily read his new book under the tree, but he soon slept. 3. Alas! They slowly walked to their old school in the rain, and they laughed. 4. Hurrah! We bravely finished our difficult homework before dinner, and we rested. 5. Wow! I carefully wrote my long essay with a pen, and I checked it. 6. Ouch! She gently closed her heavy door after lunch, but she forgot her keys. 7. Hey! You quickly drank your cold juice in the garden, and you played. 8. Bravo! He proudly showed his beautiful painting to the class, and everyone clapped.

Grammar C

' (The adjective 'responsible' follows 'is'; 'responding' is a verb form, 'responsive' means quick to react, 'responded' is past tense.)

Grammar D

i. The cat is hiding under the bed. (preposition: under) ii. She finished her homework before dinner. (verb: finished) iii. Wow! This is a beautiful dress. (interjection: Wow!) iv. He is a very good student. (adjective: good) v. She went to the store. (pronoun: She)

lessons.title: Speaking and Listening
lessons.notes_html:
Oral Communication Skills A

Present your group's findings and join a whole-class discussion. Main idea — the period of waiting ended when the Rasoolullah (peace be upon him) received Nabuwat in the cave of Hira. Supporting details — his heart overflowed with compassion for humanity; he longed to eradicate wrong beliefs, social evils, cruelty and injustice; Hazrat Jibril brought the first revelation; and the revealed words commanded reading in the name of the Lord Who created man and taught him what he knew not (Quran 96:1-5). Groups discussing other sections would follow the same pattern: state the section's main idea in one sentence, then list its supporting details from the text.

Oral Communication Skills B

i. Retelling of the first revelation — At the age of thirty-eight, Hazrat Muhammad (peace be upon him) used to retire to the cave of Hira with food and water, spending days and weeks in solitude, meditation and remembrance of Allah. One day, when the period of waiting had come to a close, Hazrat Jibril came to him in the cave and conveyed Allah's first message: 'Read in the name of thy Lord Who created, created man from a clot of congealed blood. Read, and thy Lord is the Most Bountiful, Who taught by the pen, taught man that which he knew not.' With that revelation, the divine message that would continue for twenty-three years had begun. ii. A moment of determination — When the pagan Arabs sent a delegation to his uncle Abu Talib demanding that he stop preaching or face their enmity, the Rasoolullah (peace be upon him) answered: 'My dear uncle, if they put the sun in my right hand and the moon in my left, even then I shall not abandon the proclamation of the Oneness of Allah. I shall set up the true faith upon the earth or perish in the attempt.' His uncle was so impressed that he replied, 'Son of my brother, go thy way; none will dare to touch thee. I shall never forsake thee.'

Oral Communication Skills C

i. The emotions heard in a good reader's voice depend on the passage: a passage about a struggle is read with seriousness and slow, firm pacing, while a passage about a triumph is read with warmth and rising energy. Clear pronunciation helps understanding because every word is distinct, so the listener follows the meaning instead of guessing words; correct intonation — rising for questions, pausing at commas and full stops — shows the sentence structure and the speaker's feelings. ii. and iii. are classroom activities: students practise reading aloud in pairs, give each other feedback on clarity, volume, pacing and expression, and then discuss as a class, listening respectfully and responding to others' viewpoints.

lessons.title: Writing Skills
lessons.notes_html:
Writing Skills A

Tolerance and religious harmony are essential for building positive relationships and a peaceful society. Respecting oneself and others means treating everyone with kindness and fairness, regardless of their faith, and valuing empathy and understanding over prejudice. In daily life, respect appears in small acts — listening politely to other viewpoints, celebrating each other's festivals, and refusing to mock another's beliefs — and these acts build self-esteem and self-worth in both the giver and the receiver. The benefits reach the whole society: where tolerance prevails, communities cooperate, conflicts are resolved by discussion instead of violence, and every individual feels safe to practise their religion freely. Just as the life of the Rasoolullah (peace be upon him) modelled compassion for all humanity, tolerance and religious harmony today remain the foundation of a strong, united nation. (Process notes: brainstormed ideas — kindness and fairness, self-esteem, empathy, daily-life respect, benefits for individuals and society; main idea — respect for self and others builds positive relationships and a harmonious society; mind map — centre: tolerance and religious harmony, branches: meaning, daily examples, benefits.)

Writing Skills B

Introduction — Peace and tolerance are two values on which every successful society stands: peace is the absence of conflict and the presence of justice, while tolerance is the willingness to accept people whose beliefs, customs and opinions differ from our own. Without tolerance, peace cannot last, because differences then become causes of quarrel; with tolerance, differences become a source of strength. Body — First, tolerance begins with the individual: treating others with kindness and fairness, listening before judging, and respecting every faith builds self-esteem and positive relationships. Second, tolerance benefits society: communities that respect all religions avoid sectarian conflict, cooperate in schools, workplaces and neighbourhoods, and solve disputes by discussion. History and the life of the Rasoolullah (peace be upon him) show this clearly — his compassion for all humanity and his firm stand for justice transformed a divided society into a united one. Third, intolerance has clear costs: prejudice breeds hatred, hatred breeds violence, and violence destroys the very peace in which families and economies thrive. Conclusion — Peace and tolerance must therefore be practised daily: in classrooms, in homes and in public life. A society that respects every citizen's beliefs is not merely peaceful; it is strong, united and prepared for progress.

lessons.title: Reading the Text
lessons.notes_html:
Pre-reading

L (Learned) — Patriotism means love for the motherland and devotion to one's country, and a patriot is willing to sacrifice when the need arises; the word comes from the Latin 'patriota' (countryman); a patriot's supreme values are sovereignty, integrity and honour, on which no compromise can be made; in the wars of 1965, 1971 and Kargil 1999, soldiers such as Captain Muhammad Sarwar, Major Raja Aziz Bhatti, Pilot Officer Rashid Minhas and Captain Karnal Sher Khan embraced martyrdom and were awarded Nishan-e-Haider, the highest military award.

Reading and Critical Thinking A

I define patriotism as love for the motherland combined with a willingness to sacrifice for it and to serve it honestly in daily life. The text defines it the same way: a patriot loves his country and is willing to sacrifice when the need arises. An everyday example is a student who keeps the school and neighbourhood clean, respects the law, helps neighbours in need and studies hard to become a useful citizen — small, daily acts that serve the country just as surely as a soldier's sacrifice defends it.

Reading and Critical Thinking A

Quaid-e-Azam was a nation builder and great patriot who wanted to protect the values, culture and traditions of the Muslims of the subcontinent. Without his leadership, the Muslims would have had no united voice or political direction; he gave them a sense of identity and galvanized them into a united and strong nation, as his own words say: 'We must develop a sense of patriotism which galvanizes us all into a united and strong nation.' His efforts turned the demand for a separate homeland from an idea into a political reality, securing Pakistan.

Reading and Critical Thinking A

The soldiers named in the text — Naik Saif Ali Janjua, Captain Muhammad Sarwar, Major Tufail Muhammad, Major Raja Aziz Bhatti, Pilot Officer Rashid Minhas, Major Shabbir Sharif, Sowar Muhammad Hussain, Major Muhammad Akram, Lance Naik Muhammad Mahfuz, Havildar Lalak Jan and Captain Karnal Sher Khan — are considered heroes because they laid down their lives in the wars of 1965, 1971 and Kargil 1999 to protect the homeland, and were awarded Nishan-e-Haider, the highest military award. They show courage, sacrifice, devotion to the motherland, and an uncompromising commitment to the country's sovereignty, integrity and honour.

Reading and Critical Thinking A

The spirit of patriotism can be maintained by practising it in modern, everyday forms: obeying the law, paying taxes honestly, keeping public places clean, voting responsibly, supporting Pakistani products and talent, helping fellow citizens in floods or crises, and representing Pakistan positively online instead of spreading negativity. Schools can foster it by teaching national history and the sacrifices of heroes, and by celebrating national days meaningfully. Global connection need not weaken patriotism: a Pakistani student studying abroad who speaks proudly of Pakistan, or a programmer earning foreign exchange for the country, is practising modern patriotism — serving the homeland while engaging with the world.

Reading and Critical Thinking A

Scott quotes the lines: 'Breathes there the man, with soul so dead, / Who never to himself hath said, / This is my own, my native land!' By 'a man devoid of patriotic spirit' he means a person who feels no love or attachment for his native land at all — someone whose soul is, in his words, 'dead' to the feeling every person should have for home. I agree in the sense that love for one's homeland is a natural, noble human feeling, and a person without it loses an important bond with his community and heritage. I would add, however, that true patriotism must be constructive — serving the country honestly and respecting others — rather than hatred of other nations, which Scott's lines do not advocate.

Reading and Critical Thinking A

Schools can teach patriotism by teaching national history and the stories of heroes such as the Nishan-e-Haider recipients, by celebrating national days with understanding rather than mere ceremony, by encouraging civic responsibility (cleanliness, honesty, helping others), and by giving students roles in school and community service. It is important because students are the future citizens: if they learn love for the country, respect for its values and willingness to serve it, they will grow into responsible adults who protect the nation's sovereignty, integrity and honour instead of harming them.

Reading and Critical Thinking A

A small daily act of patriotism is to keep your surroundings clean and to obey the law — for example, not littering, following traffic rules, and being honest in small dealings. It helps the country because a clean, law-abiding society is healthier, safer and more attractive for everyone, and because millions of small honest acts add up to national discipline and progress. Another daily act is studying sincerely: an educated, skilled citizen contributes far more to the nation's strength than one who wastes the opportunity.

Reading and Critical Thinking A

I learned that patriotism is not just a feeling but a live spirit that continuously inspires and guides a nation. It means love for the motherland and devotion to one's country, with a willingness to sacrifice when needed; its supreme values are sovereignty, integrity and honour, on which no compromise can be made. I learned how Quaid-e-Azam galvanized the Muslims into a united nation and secured a separate homeland, and how soldiers in the wars of 1965, 1971 and Kargil 1999 gave their lives and earned Nishan-e-Haider. Finally, I learned that patriotism must stay alert — the spirit of patriotism keeps a nation ready to defend itself against foreign invasion.

Reading and Critical Thinking B

The word 'patriot' originates from the Latin word 'patriota'.

Reading and Critical Thinking B

Patriotism. — what is considered a commendable quality according to the text.

Reading and Critical Thinking B

Quaid-e-Azam Muhammad Ali Jinnah. — who led the Muslims of the subcontinent in their struggle for a separate homeland.

Reading and Critical Thinking B

Sovereignty, integrity and honour. — what are the supreme values for a patriot according to the text.

Reading and Critical Thinking B

The wars of 1965, 1971, and the Kargil War 1999. — in which wars did many brave soldiers lay down their lives for Pakistan.

Reading and Critical Thinking C

Read the following sentence and identify the cause and effect: 'Patriots render sacrifice for the preservation and protection of the country's values.' Cause: The country's values — its sovereignty, integrity and honour — need preservation and protection (they are threatened or must be defended). Effect: Patriots render (offer) great sacrifice to preserve and protect them.

Reading and Critical Thinking C

Read the following sentence and identify the cause and effect: 'During the wars of 1965 and 1971, many soldiers displayed great courage.' Cause: Pakistan faced foreign invasion and war in 1965 and 1971, so the homeland needed defence. Effect: Many soldiers displayed great courage, laying down their lives to protect the homeland.

Reading and Critical Thinking D

Opinion. — read the following statement and identify whether it is a fact or an opinion: 'Patriotism is a commendable quality.'.

Reading and Critical Thinking D

Fact. — read the following statement and identify whether it is a fact or an opinion: 'Many soldiers were awarded Nishan-e-Haider for their bravery.'.

Reading and Critical Thinking E

Generalized statement. — read the following sentence and identify whether it is a generalized statement or evidence-based information: 'Many soldiers showed great bravery during the wars of 1965 and 1971.'.

Reading and Critical Thinking E

Evidence-based information. — read the following sentence and identify whether it is a generalized statement or evidence-based information: 'Major Tufail Muhammad was awarded Nishan-e-Haider for his bravery in the 1965 War.'.

Reading and Critical Thinking F

Patriotism requires sacrifice. — reread paragraph 2 of the unit: What is the main idea of the text.

Reading and Critical Thinking F

Identify two values that are of supreme importance to a patriot according to the text. Two supreme values are sovereignty and integrity (the third named in the text is honour). For a patriot, these values are supreme and no compromise can be made on them.

Reading and Critical Thinking F

Patriots render great sacrifice for the preservation and protection of these values — they give their strength and courage to safeguard the interests of the country and nation, and, as the soldiers of 1965, 1971 and Kargil showed, they are willing to lay down their lives for the homeland.

Reading and Critical Thinking F

Yes, the text presents a strong argument. It begins with a clear definition (love for the motherland, willingness to sacrifice), states the supreme values (sovereignty, integrity, honour), and then supports the argument with concrete evidence: Quaid-e-Azam's nation-building, the named Nishan-e-Haider martyrs of three wars, and Scott's poetic lines on the man without patriotic spirit. The combination of definition, historical example and emotional appeal makes the case convincing. A possible weakness is that the text gives only one side — it does not discuss how patriotism can be misused — but as an argument for patriotism's importance, it is well supported.

lessons.title: Vocabulary
lessons.notes_html:
Vocabulary A

Deduce the inferred meanings of these words using context clues from the text: render, sacrifice, sovereignty, commendable. render — Inferred meaning: to give or offer something (patriots 'render great sacrifice' — they give their sacrifice for the country). sacrifice — to give up something valuable, even one's life, for a greater cause (soldiers laid down their lives). sovereignty — the supreme power and independence of a country, its right to govern itself without outside control (listed with integrity and honour as supreme values). commendable — deserving praise and approval (patriotism 'is considered a commendable quality').

Vocabulary B

Use a dictionary to find the following information for each word: pronunciation, dictionary meaning, part of speech, etymology. Words: render, sacrifice, sovereignty, commendable. render — Pronunciation: /REN-der/ (/ˈrendər/). Meaning: to give, present or provide something; to cause someone or something to be in a particular state. Part of speech: verb. Etymology: from Latin 'reddere' (to give back). — sacrifice — Pronunciation: /SAK-ruh-fys/ (/ˈsækrɪfaɪs/). Meaning: the act of giving up something valuable for the sake of something else; an offering to a god. Part of speech: noun (also verb: to sacrifice). Etymology: from Latin 'sacrificium' (sacer 'sacred' + facere 'to make'). — sovereignty — Pronunciation: /SOV-rin-tee/ (/ˈsɒvrənti/). Meaning: supreme power or authority, especially of a state to govern itself. Part of speech: noun. Etymology: from Old French 'soverainete', from Latin 'superanus' (supreme). — commendable — Pronunciation: /kuh-MEN-duh-bul/ (/kəˈmendəbl/). Meaning: deserving praise and approval. Part of speech: adjective. Etymology: from Latin 'commendabilis', from 'commendare' (to entrust, praise).

Vocabulary C

The dictionary definitions confirm the inferences. 'Render' as 'to give or provide' matches the text's 'render great sacrifice'. 'Sacrifice' as 'giving up something valuable' matches the soldiers giving their lives. 'Sovereignty' as 'supreme power of a state to govern itself' matches its place among the supreme values no compromise can be made on. 'Commendable' as 'deserving praise' matches the text's judgement that patriotism is a commendable quality. The inferences were therefore accurate, and the dictionary adds precision (for example, the etymology showing 'sacrifice' comes from 'sacred making').

Vocabulary D

Use a dictionary to find and write the different word patterns for the word 'sovereignty'. Complete the chart by identifying the correct forms of the word 'sovereignty' and its related forms. Base word: sovereignty. Noun form: sovereignty (the supreme power of a state); sovereign (a monarch or ruler). Verb form: there is no standard verb form of 'sovereignty' in English (it cannot be made into a verb without changing the word). Adjective form: sovereign (having supreme power; e.g. a sovereign state). Adverb form: sovereignly (in a sovereign manner; rare in general use). Note: the verb column cannot honestly be filled from standard usage and is marked as not applicable.

Vocabulary E

Noun (sovereignty): Pakistan defends its sovereignty with great determination. Noun (sovereign): The sovereign addressed the nation on Independence Day. Adjective (sovereign): Every sovereign state has the right to make its own laws. Adverb (sovereignly, rare): The state acts sovereignly in matters of national defence. (No verb sentence is given, because 'sovereignty' has no standard verb form.)

lessons.title: Grammar Focus
lessons.notes_html:
Grammar (Tenses)

Simple present (daily routine): 1. I wake up at six o'clock every morning. 2. I offer my prayers and eat breakfast. 3. I go to school by bus. 4. I study my lessons in the evening. 5. I sleep early at night. — Simple past (last weekend): Last weekend, I visited my grandparents in the village. We played cricket in the evening, and my grandmother cooked my favourite food. I enjoyed the trip very much. — Simple future (upcoming holidays): I will visit Murree during the holidays. I will take photographs and enjoy the cool weather with my family. — Present continuous (at this moment): I am writing my English homework at this moment. — Past continuous (yesterday at this time): At this time yesterday, I was playing hockey in the school ground. — Future continuous (this time next week): At this time next week, I will be travelling to Lahore with my family.

Grammar (Perfect Tenses)

Present perfect: I have visited the Badshahi Mosque twice. She has lived in this city for ten years. — Past perfect: I had finished my homework before dinner yesterday evening. They had completed their project before the teacher arrived. — Future perfect: I will have graduated from school by next year. She will have completed her primary education by the end of this year. — Present perfect continuous: I have been working on my science project for the last three weeks. She has been studying for three hours. — Past perfect continuous: He had been working at the company for five years before he left. I had been reading this novel for a week before the exams began. — Future perfect continuous: By the next month, she will have been working here for a year. By next June, I will have been studying English for five years.

Grammar A

Read the following passage carefully. Underline the verbs and identify their tenses. Passage: 'Every morning, Maria walks to school. Yesterday, she walked with her friend because her bike was broken. Tomorrow, she will ride her bike again. Maria has been attending this school for three years, and she loves it. By the end of this year, she will have completed her primary education.' walks — Simple Present (habitual action, every morning). walked — Simple Past (yesterday). was — Simple Past (linking verb; 'was broken' is past passive). will ride — Simple Future (tomorrow). has been attending — Present Perfect Continuous (started in the past, continuing for three years). loves — Simple Present (general truth/feeling). will have completed — Future Perfect (completed before a future time, the end of this year).

Grammar B

Dear Diary, Today was a busy day. I woke up early (Simple Past) and now I am writing this entry before sleeping (Present Continuous). I go to school every day (Simple Present), and I have been preparing for my exams for two weeks (Present Perfect Continuous). Tomorrow, I will revise all my lessons (Simple Future), and by the end of this month, I will have completed my syllabus (Future Perfect). I had finished my homework before dinner yesterday (Past Perfect), so today I felt relaxed. It was a good day!

Grammar C

Read the events listed below. Identify the tense used in each event. Place the events on the timeline in the correct sequence based on their tenses and the given dates. Events: 1. I will have graduated from the university by next June. 2. I am studying for my exams right now. 3. I visited Karachi two years ago. 4. I have been working on my project for the last three weeks. 5. I had finished my homework before dinner yesterday evening. Tenses: 1. Future Perfect (completed before next June). 2. Present Continuous (right now). 3. Simple Past (two years ago). 4. Present Perfect Continuous (started three weeks ago, continuing). 5. Past Perfect (completed before dinner yesterday). Correct timeline sequence (earliest to latest): 3 (two years ago) → 5 (yesterday evening, before dinner) → 4 (last three weeks up to now) → 2 (right now) → 1 (by next June).

Grammar D

Read the following sentences. Underline the gerunds, infinitives, and participles and label them accordingly. 1. Swimming is my favourite hobby. 2. To learn a new language takes time. 3. The broken window needs to be fixed. 4. She enjoys reading books. 5. To travel around the world is my dream. 6. The running water creates a sweet sound. 1. Swimming — gerund (the -ing form used as the subject, a noun). 2. To learn — infinitive (to + base verb used as the subject). 3. broken — past participle (used as an adjective describing 'window'). 4. reading — gerund (the -ing form used as the object of 'enjoys'). 5. To travel — infinitive (used as the subject). 6. running — present participle (used as an adjective describing 'water').

Grammar E

Transform the following base verbs into gerunds, infinitives, and participles. Use each form in a sentence. Base verbs: write, play, eat. write — Gerund: Writing is a useful skill. (Writing improves with practice.) Infinitive: To write well, you must read widely. Present participle: The writing student did not hear the bell. Past participle: The written essay was praised by the teacher. — play — Gerund: Playing hockey keeps me fit. Infinitive: To play fairly is more important than to win. Present participle: The playing children laughed loudly. Past participle: The played match was very exciting. — eat — Gerund: Eating vegetables is healthy. Infinitive: To eat on time is a good habit. Present participle: The eating guests enjoyed the dinner. Past participle: The eaten food was delicious.

Grammar F

Swimming (gerund) is my favourite hobby, and I enjoy reading (gerund) books about great swimmers. To learn (infinitive) a new skill takes patience, and to travel (infinitive) for competitions is my dream. The running (present participle) water in the pool looked inviting, and the broken (past participle) starting block reminded me to be careful. (Gerunds: Swimming, reading. Infinitives: To learn, to travel. Participles: running — present participle; broken — past participle.)

lessons.notes_html:
Writing Skills A

My service to society begins with small, sincere actions in my own surroundings. I keep my street clean, help elderly neighbours with their work, and tutor younger children in my neighbourhood who struggle with their lessons. At school, I take part in cleanliness drives and plantation campaigns, because a green, clean environment benefits everyone. I also obey the law, speak politely to all, and use social media to spread useful information rather than rumours. I believe that serving society does not require wealth or power; it requires a willing heart, honest conduct and regular small deeds, and if every citizen serves in this way, the whole society becomes stronger, kinder and more prosperous.

Introduction — I love Pakistan because it is my homeland, the country my forefathers struggled to create, and the land where I was born and raised. Its green fields, high mountains, rivers and deserts are beautiful, but what I love most is its people and its values. Body — First, Pakistan was created through great sacrifice: Quaid-e-Azam Muhammad Ali Jinnah led the Muslims of the subcontinent to a separate homeland where they could live according to their faith and culture. Second, its heroes inspire me: soldiers who gave their lives in 1965, 1971 and Kargil, and were awarded Nishan-e-Haider, showed what love for the country truly means. Third, Pakistan's culture — its languages, hospitality, sports and arts — fills me with pride. Conclusion — Loving Pakistan is not only a feeling; it is a duty. I will serve my country by studying hard, obeying the law, keeping it clean and helping my fellow citizens, so that Pakistan grows stronger and more prosperous.

lessons.title: Reading the Text
lessons.notes_html:
Reading and Critical Thinking A

The central idea is nature's lasting joy through memory — the bliss of solitude. The poet, wandering lonely as a cloud, sees a host of golden daffodils beside a lake; the sight fills him with joy at the time, and later, when he lies on his couch in a vacant or pensive mood, the memory of the daffodils flashes upon his inward eye and his heart dances with them again. Nature's beauty thus gives happiness twice: once in the experience and again in recollection.

Reading and Critical Thinking A

The poet saw the daffodils beside a lake, beneath the trees, in a never-ending line along the margin of a bay. The poem was inspired by a walk Wordsworth took with his sister Dorothy near Ullswater in the Lake District on 15 April 1802. The open, peaceful lakeside setting, with the flowers stretching endlessly along the bay, creates a mood of calm wonder and joyful freedom, and makes the golden flowers stand out vividly against the blue water and sky.

Reading and Critical Thinking A

The poet describes a crowd, a host of golden daffodils, fluttering and dancing in the breeze, tossing their heads in sprightly dance. He uses visual imagery of gold (golden daffodils), number (ten thousand saw he at a glance), and movement (fluttering, dancing, tossing heads). He compares them to stars that shine and twinkle on the Milky Way, stretched in a never-ending line, and says the sparkling waves danced too, but the flowers outdid them in glee — imagery that makes the scene feel alive, joyful and endless.

Reading and Critical Thinking A

Give examples. Personification gives the daffodils human life and joy, which is what makes them companions for the lonely poet. Examples: the daffodils are 'fluttering and dancing in the breeze' and 'tossing their heads in sprightly dance' — actions of lively dancers; the waves 'danced' beside them; the flowers form a 'jocund company' — cheerful companions; and in the last stanza the poet's heart 'dances with the daffodils'. By making the flowers dance and keep company, Wordsworth turns a landscape into a living, joyful presence that cures loneliness.

Reading and Critical Thinking A

The poem is written in four six-line stanzas with the rhyme scheme ABABCC in each stanza (for example, in stanza 1: cloud/crowd, hills/daffodils, trees/breeze). The steady, flowing rhythm and the regular rhyming couplets at the end of each stanza give the poem a song-like, musical quality. This musical flow matches the dancing movement of the daffodils themselves, so the sound of the poem feels as joyful and graceful as the scene it describes.

Reading and Critical Thinking A

'Jocund company' means cheerful, merry companions. The poet calls the daffodils a jocund company because their dancing presence gave him joy and cured his loneliness: at the sight of them he gazed in wonder, not knowing what wealth the show had brought him, and later, in memory, they again fill his heart with pleasure. The phrase reflects his feeling that the flowers were not mere plants but joyful friends whose company lifted his spirits twice — once in the moment and once in recollection.

Reading and Critical Thinking A

Explain the concept of 'bliss of solitude' as presented in the poem. The 'bliss of solitude' is the joyful peace of being alone, made happy by a beautiful memory. In the last stanza, when the poet lies on his couch 'in vacant or in pensive mood' — alone, with an empty or thoughtful mind — the daffodils 'flash upon that inward eye', the eye of memory and imagination. His heart then fills with pleasure and dances with the daffodils. Solitude here is not sad loneliness; it is a chosen, peaceful aloneness that memory turns into bliss, because the beauty once seen in nature lives on in the mind.

Reading and Critical Thinking A

The themes apply whenever a beautiful moment in nature stays with us and comforts us later. Like the poet, we can carry memories of a garden, a riverside, mountains or rain into lonely or difficult times, and let them lift our hearts. For example, on a quiet evening I remembered a spring morning when I walked among yellow flowers in a park; recalling their colour and movement made me smile and feel peaceful, just as the daffodils made the poet's heart dance. The poem teaches us to notice nature closely, because what we truly notice becomes a lasting source of joy.

Reading and Critical Thinking B

The beauty of nature. — what is the main theme of the poem 'Daffodils'.

Reading and Critical Thinking B

Reading and Critical Thinking B

Beside a lake. — where did the poet see the daffodils.

Reading and Critical Thinking B

Fluttering and dancing. — how are the daffodils described in the poem.

Reading and Critical Thinking B

A starry night. — the daffodils are compared to:.

Reading and Critical Thinking B

Tens of thousands. — how many daffodils did the poet see at a glance.

Reading and Critical Thinking B

The poet was feeling lonely when he saw the daffodils.

Reading and Critical Thinking B

Bring him joy. — what do the daffodils do for the poet when he is alone.

Reading and Critical Thinking B

In a vacant or in pensive mood. — in what mood does the poet lie on his couch in the last stanza.

lessons.title: Vocabulary
lessons.notes_html:
Vocabulary A

'Lonely' and 'solitary' have similar denotations but different connotations. Work out the difference from the poem's use of 'lonely', and explain how the tone would change if 'solitary' were used instead. Denotation (dictionary meaning) is almost the same: both mean being alone. Connotation differs: 'lonely' carries a negative, sad feeling — being alone and feeling the lack of company — while 'solitary' is neutral or even positive, suggesting peaceful aloneness by choice. The poem needs 'lonely' in the opening line ('I wandered lonely as a cloud') because the poet's sadness is what the daffodils transform into joy; if 'solitary' were used, the opening would feel calm rather than sad, and the transformation from loneliness to joy would lose its contrast and emotional force.

Vocabulary B

Identify the denotative and connotative meanings of the following words from the poem: lonely, cloud, fluttering, sprightly, gazed, bliss. lonely — Denotative: alone, without company. Connotative: sad, isolated, longing for company (the poet's opening mood). — cloud — Denotative: a visible mass of water vapour in the sky. Connotative: drifting, free, aimless wandering high above the world (the poet floats 'lonely as a cloud'). — fluttering — Denotative: moving lightly and quickly, as wings or leaves in air. Connotative: joyful, lively, delicate movement (the daffodils' dance). — sprightly — Denotative: lively, full of energy. Connotative: cheerful, youthful high spirits (the daffodils 'tossing their heads in sprightly dance'). — gazed — Denotative: looked steadily and intently. Connotative: a wonder-filled, absorbed look (the poet 'gazed — and gazed' at the wealth of the show). — bliss — Denotative: perfect happiness, great joy. Connotative: deep, peaceful, almost spiritual happiness (the 'bliss of solitude').

Vocabulary C

Compare the connotations of each pair and explain the tone each word creates: gaze / stare; shine / glare; hoard / collect. gaze (positive) vs stare (negative): 'gaze' suggests a steady, admiring, thoughtful look — the poet gazes at the daffodils with wonder; 'stare' suggests a rude, fixed, unfriendly look. Tone: gaze is gentle and appreciative; stare is harsh and intrusive. — shine (positive) vs glare (negative): 'shine' suggests bright, pleasant light — the stars 'shine and twinkle'; 'glare' suggests harsh, dazzling, uncomfortable light. Tone: shine is warm and beautiful; glare is aggressive and unpleasant. — hoard (negative) vs collect (positive): 'hoard' suggests selfishly piling things up and refusing to share; 'collect' suggests gathering with interest and care, often to enjoy or preserve. Tone: hoard is greedy and secretive; collect is orderly and appreciative.

lessons.title: Grammar Focus
lessons.notes_html:
Grammar A

Identify the figures of speech in the following lines and explain their effect: 1. 'I wandered lonely as a cloud.' 2. 'Fluttering and dancing in the breeze.' / 'Tossing their heads in sprightly dance.' 3. 'Ten thousand saw I at a glance.' 4. 'They flash upon that inward eye.' 5. 'Beside the lake, beneath the trees.' 6. The comparison of daffodils to stars that shine and twinkle on the Milky Way. 1. Simile — 'lonely as a cloud': the poet compares himself to a cloud using 'as'; it shows his free, drifting, solitary wandering high above the valleys and hills. 2. Personification — the daffodils flutter, dance and toss their heads like lively human dancers; it makes the flowers feel alive and joyful, turning them into cheerful company. 3. Hyperbole — 'ten thousand' is a deliberate exaggeration; it stresses the vast, countless number of flowers stretching in a never-ending line. 4. Metaphor — the 'inward eye' is the mind's eye, memory and imagination; it shows that the poet sees the daffodils again inwardly, in recollection. 5. Alliteration — the repeated 'b' sounds in 'Beside the lake, beneath the trees' give the line a soft, musical flow. 6. Simile and imagery — the daffodils are 'continuous as the stars that shine / And twinkle on the Milky Way'; the star imagery stresses their vast number, golden brightness and heavenly beauty, and fills the scene with wonder.

Grammar B

Her smile is like the sun. — which of the following is a simile.

Grammar B

Personification. — identify the figure of speech: 'The flowers danced in the breeze.'.

Grammar B

The classroom was a zoo. — which is an example of a metaphor.

Grammar B

Simile. — 'Her cheeks are as red as an apple' is an example of:.

Grammar B

I am so hungry I could eat a horse. — which sentence uses hyperbole.

Grammar B

Metaphor. — 'Time is a great healer' is an example of:.

Grammar B

She sells seashells. — which of the following shows alliteration.

Grammar C

Wordsworth chose similes and personification because they make the scene feel alive and emotional rather than merely described. The simile 'lonely as a cloud' lets us feel his solitude; personification — the flowers dancing and tossing their heads — turns the daffodils into joyful companions, which is exactly what the poem's theme requires: nature as a living friend whose memory brings joy. Plain description would tell us what the flowers looked like; figures of speech let us feel what they meant to the poet.

Grammar C

Euphemism (softening harsh things) and oxymoron (joining opposite ideas, like 'sweet sorrow') would break the poem's pure, uplifting tone. The poem celebrates unmixed joy and the healing power of a beautiful memory; an oxymoron would introduce contradiction and tension, and a euphemism would soften or hide feelings that the poem wants to express openly. The joyful similes and personification keep the tone harmonious, bright and sincere, matching the golden daffodils themselves.

Grammar C

Give a reason. No. Oxymoron does not always create a negative or confusing effect; it can add depth by holding two truths together, as in 'bittersweet' (joy mixed with sadness) or 'deafening silence' (silence so complete it feels loud). Its effect depends on purpose: in a poem about mixed feelings it can be powerful, but in 'Daffodils', where the feeling is pure joy, an oxymoron would have weakened the clarity of that joy, which is why Wordsworth does not use one.

Grammar C

A writer should use euphemism when a topic is painful, embarrassing or sensitive and a gentler expression shows respect — for example, saying someone 'passed away' instead of 'died' when speaking to a grieving family. A writer should avoid euphemism when clarity and honesty matter more than softness, or when the feeling itself is the point: in 'Daffodils', Wordsworth wants the joy stated plainly and brightly, so softening or hiding it behind gentle words would weaken the poem. Rule: use euphemism to be kind about harsh subjects; avoid it when directness serves truth or emotion better.

Grammar D

According to the weather report, it will rain tomorrow the weather report, it will rain tomorrow.

Grammar D

The dog stood The dog stood in front of the gate, waiting for its owner the gate, waiting for its owner.

Grammar D

She spoke She spoke on behalf of her friend, who could not attend the meeting. ('On behalf of' means 'representing someone'.) her friend, who could not attend the meeting.

Grammar D

The match was cancelled The match was cancelled due to heavy rain heavy rain.

Grammar D

In addition to the main course, we were served dessert the main course, we were served dessert.

Grammar D

In spite of the rain, we decided to go for a walk the rain, we decided to go for a walk.

Grammar E

According to — According to my teacher, regular practice improves English. In front of — The school bus stopped in front of the main gate. On behalf of — The monitor collected the homework on behalf of the class. Due to — The match was postponed due to bad weather. In addition to — In addition to English, I am learning Arabic. In spite of — In spite of the heat, the players finished the match.

Grammar F

' about a verb is an adverb phrase.

Grammar G

In the morning — In the morning, I revise my lessons before school. Under the bed — The cat hid under the bed during the storm. With a smile — The teacher greeted us with a smile. After the game — After the game, we thanked the visiting team. On the roof — The kites were flying above the houses, but one landed on the roof. Oral Communication Skills Oral: Read the following stanza from 'Arrival of the Monsoon' by Taufiq Rafat and answer: What is the main idea of the stanza? What imagery does the poet use? (Stanza: 'And the first rain, / the first rain, / alive, alive, / the wire swinging / in the rain, / the brown waters / round the hooves, / the drenched trees / shaking off the rain, / the summer ending / in drops of rain.') Main idea: the arrival of the monsoon revives everything — the first rain brings new life after the dry summer, and the whole landscape wakes up. Imagery: the repeated word 'alive, alive' stresses new life; the wire swinging in the rain gives a visual image of wind and rain together; the brown waters round the hooves show flooded fields and animals standing in rainwater; the drenched trees shaking off the rain show trees shaking themselves dry like living creatures; and 'the summer ending in drops of rain' is a gentle closing image of one season dissolving into another. Like Wordsworth's daffodils, the monsoon scene is nature made vivid and alive.

lessons.title: Writing Skills
lessons.notes_html:
Writing Skills A

Last stanza: 'For oft, when on my couch I lie / In vacant or in pensive mood, / They flash upon that inward eye / Which is the bliss of solitude; / And then my heart with pleasure fills, / And dances with the daffodils.' Often, when I lie resting on my sofa with an empty or thoughtful mind, the daffodils suddenly appear before my mind's eye — that inner vision which is the joyful blessing of being peacefully alone. Then my heart fills with happiness, and it dances along with the daffodils in my memory, just as they danced beside the lake.

Writing Skills B

'Daffodils' by William Wordsworth describes the poet wandering alone like a cloud when he suddenly sees a large number of golden daffodils beside a lake, beneath the trees, stretching in a never-ending line along the bay. The key imagery presents the flowers fluttering and dancing in the breeze, tossing their heads in sprightly dance, compared in number and brightness to stars shining and twinkling on the Milky Way; the sparkling waves dance too, but the daffodils outdo them in joy. The main idea is that nature's beauty gives lasting joy through memory: when the poet later lies on his couch in a vacant or pensive mood, the daffodils flash upon his inward eye — the bliss of solitude — and his heart fills with pleasure and dances with the daffodils.

lessons.title: Reading the Text
lessons.notes_html:
Pre-reading

In my family, my mother plays the central role in making us happy and successful. She manages the home, prepares our food, looks after our health and studies, and keeps the family united with patience and kindness. Like Hazrat Asma (RA), who supported her father and the Rasoolullah (SAW) during the migration with courage and service, a mother serves her family quietly every day; her sacrifices, prayers and guidance are the foundation of the family's happiness and success.

Pre-reading

Yes. Hazrat Asma (RA) was the daughter of Hazrat Abu Bakr Siddique (RA), the elder sister of Hazrat Ayesha Siddiqua (RA), the wife of Hazrat Zubair bin al-Awwam (RA) and the mother of Hazrat Abdullah bin Zubair (RA). She is famous for her services during the migration (Hijrat) of 622 A.D., when she prepared food for the journey, tied it on the camel's back with her own belt, and earned the title of Zaat-un-Nitaqain from the Rasoolullah (SAW). She was known for her courage, generosity, wisdom and resolute faith.

While-reading

The Rasoolullah (SAW) and his close companion, Hazrat Abu Bakr Siddique (RA), migrated from Makkah Mukarramah to Madinah Munawwarah in the year 622 A.D.

While-reading

She was given the title of Zaat-un-Nitaqain (the one with two belts/waistbands) by the Rasoolullah (SAW). The reason: she prepared food for the journey and, as nothing else could be found to tie it with, she tied the food on the camel's back with her own belt — using her belt as the binding, an act of resourcefulness that earned her this honoured title.

While-reading

' She made no statement that would give him even a minor clue. Abu Jehl was infuriated and slapped her face so hard that her ear-ring fell off, but she remained steadfast and did not reveal the secret.

While-reading

Her grandfather, Hazrat Abu Quhafaa (RA), who was very old and blind and a disbeliever at that time, feared that Abu Bakr had taken all the wealth, leaving Asma and the children empty-handed and helpless. Hazrat Asma (RA) instantly ran to a corner of the home, gathered some pebbles, put them at the place where her father used to keep his money and jewels, covered them with a piece of cloth, and said, 'Come grandfather, look! He has left all this for us.' He touched the cloth, thought it was full of gold and jewels, and his concern was alleviated; he felt relieved that his son had left all his wealth at home.

While-reading

List all the family relations of Hazrat Asma (RA) as mentioned in the text. Daughter of Hazrat Abu Bakr Siddique (RA); stepsister of Hazrat Ayesha Siddiqua (RA); wife of Hazrat Zubair bin al-Awwam (RA); mother of Hazrat Abdullah bin Zubair (RA); granddaughter of Hazrat Abu Quhafaa (RA); aunt of Hazrat Abdullah bin Zubair's children (her son said he had not seen anybody more generous than his aunt Hazrat Ayesha (RA) and his mother — the text presents Hazrat Ayesha (RA) as the aunt in that remark). She was amongst the early few who had accepted Islam, and she died at the old age of about a hundred years.

Reading and Critical Thinking A

Provide specific examples from the text. Her resourcefulness is shown when, finding nothing else to tie the journey's food with, she used her own belt to tie the food on the camel's back — the act that earned her the title of Zaat-un-Nitaqain. Her courage is shown in the perilous nightly task itself: every night, with a pack of food, she ventured quietly towards the rugged mountains where the cave of Thawr was located, traversing the rocky path at night with the constant fear of being detected and caught, when even the slightest mistake could have endangered the life of the Rasoolullah (SAW). Further courage is shown in her wise, polite counter-question to the furious Abu Jehl, and in remaining steadfast after being slapped so hard that her ear-ring fell off, without revealing the secret.

Reading and Critical Thinking A

Her qualities apply whenever a person is trusted with something valuable and must protect it honestly under pressure. For example, a student who is trusted with the class funds for a trip must keep an exact record, spend only on the agreed purpose, and refuse to misuse even a small amount — just as Hazrat Asma (RA) protected the secret of her father's whereabouts and safeguarded her family's trust. Another example is an employee who finds a lost wallet at work and returns it untouched, or a child who tells the truth to a parent even when telling the truth is difficult. In all these cases, trust and integrity mean doing the right thing even when no one is watching, as Hazrat Asma (RA) did.

Reading and Critical Thinking A

Summarize the key challenges Hazrat Asma (RA) faced during the migration and how she overcame them. Challenges: (1) The chiefs of Makkah were furious at the migration, offered huge rewards and bounties for the capture of the Rasoolullah (SAW) and Hazrat Abu Bakr (RA), dead or alive, and were more determined than ever to find them. (2) Supplying food during the perilous journey was extremely difficult, because the situation was so delicate that the slightest mistake could endanger the Rasoolullah's (SAW) life. (3) She had to traverse the rocky path at night with the constant fear of detection and capture. (4) Abu Jehl confronted her violently, demanding her father's whereabouts, and slapped her face so hard that her ear-ring fell off. (5) Her blind, elderly grandfather feared the family had been left empty-handed. She overcame them by careful preparation (food tied with her own belt), nightly quiet venturing to the cave of Thawr with attention to minute details, a wise counter-question that revealed nothing, steadfast silence under violence, and a creative, kind solution for her grandfather with pebbles under a cloth.

Reading and Critical Thinking A

She handled the trust in three ways: by preparing food and supplies at her father's house for the journey; by carrying food every night to the cave of Thawr, quietly and carefully, so that the travellers could survive in hiding; and by guarding the secret of their whereabouts absolutely — giving Abu Jehl no clue even under violence. These actions ensured safety and success because the migration depended on secrecy and supply: without food, the travellers could not remain hidden, and without silence, the searchers with their bounties would have found them. Her trustworthiness therefore protected both the lives of the Rasoolullah (SAW) and Hazrat Abu Bakr (RA) and the whole plan of the Hijrat.

Reading and Critical Thinking A

Her self-discipline is visible in her careful, repeated routine: preparing the food, attending to minute details, and venturing out every night on the same dangerous path without panic or carelessness. Self-discipline gave her control over fear — she moved quietly, kept the secret, and answered Abu Jehl politely rather than angrily or fearfully. Because she disciplined her words and actions, she never gave the enemy a clue, never failed in the nightly supply, and never let hardship shake her faith. Her resolute faith in Allah and her disciplined conduct together turned dangerous situations into successful ones.

She also showed respect through generosity in later life, selling her inherited garden and giving all the money to the poor and needy, so that nobody ever returned empty-handed from her doorstep.

Reading and Critical Thinking A

Although her grandfather Hazrat Abu Quhafaa (RA) was a disbeliever at that time, she treated him with kindness, patience and honour: she listened to his worry, acted at once to comfort him, and used pebbles covered with cloth so that he would believe wealth had been left for the family and feel relieved. This respect aligns with her Islamic values: Islam teaches kindness and good treatment of parents and elders regardless of their faith, and her actions show modesty, truthfulness in intention (to comfort, not to harm), honesty, piety, bravery and generosity — the very qualities the unit's theme celebrates. Her respect did not compromise her faith; it expressed it.

Read the following passage carefully. Underline the verbs and identify their tenses. Passage: 'Hazrat Asma (RA) courageously faced many challenges during the migration. lessons.title: Reading the Text
lessons.notes_html:
Pre-reading

Entrepreneurship is the process of starting, managing and growing a business venture: entrepreneurs identify opportunities, take calculated risks and bring innovative ideas to life, creating products or services to meet market demands. It is important today because it creates jobs, drives economic growth, solves problems and gives people — including women — financial independence and control over their own futures.

Pre-reading

In our country, women run boutiques, bakeries, catering services, schools and online stores; globally, famous women entrepreneurs lead fashion, technology and food businesses. The unit's own example is Hazrat Khadija (RA), a prominent businesswoman of Makkah. Challenges they may face, as the unit lists, include cultural expectations that women prioritise household duties, limited access to finance, education and networks, mobility restrictions, legal and institutional barriers in registering businesses, and a lack of support networks and mentors.

Pre-reading

Women entrepreneurs improve communities by creating jobs (especially for other women and youth), providing useful goods and services, and starting businesses that address local needs such as education, healthcare and access to resources. They also serve as role models who inspire younger generations, challenge gender stereotypes, promote gender equality, and bring innovation and problem-solving into community life.

Reading and Critical Thinking A

Hazrat Khadija (RA) was one of the wealthiest individuals of her time and was known for her wisdom, integrity and leadership in managing a thriving trading business. She carefully expanded her trading ventures, conducting business across various regions, and her influence extended beyond her wealth — she became a symbol of empowerment for other women. Modern women entrepreneurs can apply the same qualities: wisdom in decision-making, integrity in dealings, leadership in managing a business, hard work, intelligence and strategic thinking, and the courage to expand carefully even when society expects otherwise. Her example shows that gender should not be a barrier to success.

Reading and Critical Thinking A

Women-led businesses contribute to economic development by creating jobs, generating income and boosting productivity, which results in a more dynamic economy that benefits everyone. They often employ people from their own communities, providing job opportunities and reducing unemployment, especially for other women and youth. In rural areas this matters even more: women in handicrafts and artisanship create handmade products like jewellery, carpets and decorative items which they sell in local markets or export, and women in education and training centres run schools, training institutes and daycare centres that serve community needs — so business growth directly becomes local employment and development.

Reading and Critical Thinking A

Mentorship and networking are critical because, unlike male entrepreneurs who have access to established business networks, women often struggle to find mentors or role models, and the absence of such support networks makes it harder to succeed in competitive markets. Mentorship programmes guide aspiring businesswomen in developing essential skills; microfinance institutions offer loans to start small businesses; and women's chambers of commerce provide platforms for female entrepreneurs to network and showcase their products. Together these systems give women finance, skills, contacts and confidence — the very resources the unit lists as often limited for women, particularly in rural areas.

Reading and Critical Thinking A

E-commerce plays a liberating role: with the rise of digital platforms, many women use technology to launch online businesses, sell products via social media or run tech startups. The growth of e-commerce and online platforms has given women more flexibility, allowing them to run businesses from their homes and bypass some of the mobility issues they face — restrictions on movement that limit their ability to meet clients, travel for business or access markets. Online selling thus lets a woman reach customers without facing the cultural and mobility barriers of physical travel.

Reading and Critical Thinking A

The success of women entrepreneurs serves as a catalyst because women entrepreneurs serve as role models for other women: by witnessing women succeed in business, younger generations are inspired to pursue their ambitions. Hazrat Khadija (RA) herself is presented as an example that has inspired generations of women to pursue their entrepreneurial dreams regardless of societal expectations. Each successful woman entrepreneur proves that barriers can be overcome, and thereby encourages the next generation to try.

Reading and Critical Thinking A

Women's entrepreneurship benefits the wider community, not only the women themselves: it creates jobs, fosters innovation and promotes gender equality. Many women entrepreneurs start businesses that address local issues such as education, healthcare or access to resources, creating a positive social impact and improving the quality of life in their communities. It can be leveraged by supporting such ventures — for example, encouraging women to open training centres and daycare centres for education, or health-related services — and by the Government and NGOs providing financial resources, training and market access, so that business success and community welfare grow together.

Reading and Critical Thinking A

Limited access to loans directly blocks women from starting or expanding businesses: many women, particularly in rural areas, have limited access to financial resources, education and networks, and banks may be hesitant to offer loans to women, while business training programmes are not always readily available. This keeps ventures small, informal or impossible. More equitable opportunities can be provided through microfinance institutions offering small loans, mentorship and training programmes, women's chambers of commerce for networking, and Government and NGO support with financial resources, training and market access — creating a more inclusive and supportive environment for female entrepreneurs.

Reading and Critical Thinking A

When women participate in the economy as entrepreneurs, they challenge gender stereotypes and promote equality: their success encourages society to view women as capable leaders and decision-makers rather than only as homemakers. By taking control of their futures, challenging societal norms and becoming leaders in their communities, women entrepreneurs break traditional gender roles. The unit's benefits list makes the point explicitly: promoting gender equality happens when women's economic participation challenges stereotypes, and the role-model effect then inspires younger generations, gradually changing what society expects of women.

Identify the idioms and proverbs in the following sentences from the provided text and explain their literal and figurative meanings: 1. Women entrepreneurs in Pakistan are making strides in various fields, despite having the odds stacked against them. 2. She carefully expanded her trading ventures, proving that slow and steady wins the race. 3. By becoming entrepreneurs, women are breaking new ground and paving the way for future generations. 4. Women, who face criticism from society, often rise above it and prove that actions speak louder than words. 5. Despite limited access to resources, women are showing that where there's a will, there's a way. 1. 'the odds stacked against them' — Idiom. Literal: the chances in a game are piled up against someone. Figurative: facing strong disadvantages and unfair difficulties (here, societal and financial barriers) yet still progressing ('making strides'). 2. 'slow and steady wins the race' — Proverb (from the tortoise and hare story). Literal: a slow, steady runner wins a race. Figurative: careful, patient, persistent effort succeeds better than hasty action — as Hazrat Khadija (RA) carefully expanded her ventures. 3. 'breaking new ground' and 'paving the way' — Idioms. Literal: breaking untouched soil; laying a road surface. Figurative: doing something never done before (women entering business), and making future progress easier for others (future generations). 4. 'rise above it' and 'actions speak louder than words' — Idiom and proverb. Literal: to rise physically above something; spoken words making a louder sound than actions. Figurative: to overcome criticism without being dragged down by it; what a person does matters more than what they claim. 5. 'where there's a will, there's a way' — Proverb. Literal: wherever determination exists, a road exists. Figurative: strong determination finds a solution despite limited resources.

After school — lunch, homework, extracurricular activities (e.g., sports practice), free time (e.g., watching TV, playing video games), dinner.
